**The Last Times**

We rarely know when we're doing something for the final time. The last time your mother carried you, she didn't announce it. Somewhere between one ordinary Tuesday and the next, you simply became too heavy, and that was that—no ceremony, no footnote in the family record. The last time you played hide-and-seek with a childhood friend ended like any other game, scattered with laughter, and then you both just... stopped, the way children drift out of things, and neither of you thought to mark the occasion.

This is the quiet cruelty of time: it takes things without telling us. We get to say goodbye to people, sometimes, if we're lucky. But we almost never get to say goodbye to the small rituals that make up a life. The last time you slept in a particular bed. The last time a certain song was your favorite. The last time you believed, fully and without irony, in Santa Claus or the goodness of a particular person or that you were invincible.

Perhaps this is why we photograph things compulsively now, why we journal, why we press flowers in books. We're trying to catch the moment in the act of ending. But the snapshot always arrives too late or too early—never at the precise instant when something is happening for the last time.

The consolation, I suppose, is that it works both ways. Somewhere in your future is a last time you haven't recognized yet, something you'll do today without knowing it matters. So do it carefully. Fold the laundry like it's an art. Call the friend. The ordinary is more fragile than it looks.
